name: agricultural_science_set2_p1
label: Agricultural Science: set 2 (crop production, propagation, cereals, legumes, roots, cash crops, vegetables and fruit)

papers.title: Principles of Crop Production: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on principles of crop production, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Making a hole with a stick and placing seeds in it, as is done for maize and groundnut, is called
questions.explanation:
Dibbling places seeds at a set spacing and depth, so the stand is even and weeding is easier than after broadcasting.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- broadcasting: Broadcasting is scattering seeds evenly by hand over the land.
- drilling: Drilling is sowing seeds in a continuous line in a furrow.
- transplanting: Transplanting is moving seedlings from a nursery to the field.

questions.stem: Maize is planted at a spacing of 80 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows, with one plant per stand. What is the plant population per hectare?
questions.explanation:
Area per plant = 0.80 m × 0.25 m = 0.2 m². Plant population = 10 000 m² ÷ 0.2 m² = 50 000 plants per hectare.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5: This divides 10 000 by 80 × 25 without first converting the spacing to metres.
- 2000: This is just 80 × 25, the area per plant in cm², not the number of plants.
- 100 000: This doubles the answer, as if there were two plants per stand.

questions.stem: Removing extra seedlings so that each stand has the right number of plants is called
questions.explanation:
Thinning reduces competition for light, water and nutrients; supplying fills the gaps. Both give an even plant population.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- supplying: Supplying is replacing seeds or seedlings that failed to grow.
- pruning: Pruning is cutting off unwanted branches of trees and shrubs.
- earthing up: Earthing up is drawing soil around the base of plants.

questions.stem: Growing maize and cowpea together in alternate rows is an example of
questions.explanation:
Intercropping places two or more crops in definite rows or patterns. The cowpea, a legume, adds nitrogen that the maize can use.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mixed cropping: In mixed cropping the crops grow together with no definite pattern.
- relay cropping: In relay cropping a second crop is planted before the first one is harvested.
- crop rotation: Crop rotation grows different crops one after another, not together.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a principle of crop rotation?
questions.explanation:
Rotation maintains fertility, breaks the life cycles of pests and diseases, and helps control weeds.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A crop should be followed by another crop of the same family: Crops of the same family share pests and diseases, so they should not follow one another.
- Shallow-rooted crops should always follow shallow-rooted crops: Deep- and shallow-rooted crops should alternate, so different soil layers are used.
- The same crop should be grown every year to build up its pests' enemies: Growing the same crop every year builds up its pests and diseases.

options.label: A
options.content: A crop should be followed by another crop of the same family

options.label: B
options.content: Shallow-rooted crops should always follow shallow-rooted crops

options.label: C
options.content: Heavy feeders such as maize should follow, or be followed by, legumes

options.label: D
options.content: The same crop should be grown every year to build up its pests' enemies

questions.stem: Crops are planted at the start of the rains mainly because
questions.explanation:
A crop planted several weeks late can lose a large part of its yield, because the rains end before it matures and pests have multiplied.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- seeds will not germinate later in the year: Seeds can germinate whenever there is moisture; late planting reduces yield, not germination.
- fertilisers work only at the start of the rains: Fertilisers work whenever there is moisture for roots to take them up.
- weeds do not grow at the start of the rains: Weeds grow vigorously when the rains start; that is why early weeding matters.

options.label: A
options.content: seeds will not germinate later in the year

options.label: B
options.content: fertilisers work only at the start of the rains

options.label: C
options.content: weeds do not grow at the start of the rains

options.label: D
options.content: the crop then has moisture for the whole season, before many pests build up

questions.stem: Weeding is most important during the first four to six weeks after planting because
questions.explanation:
Early weed competition stunts the crop and reduces yield more than later weeds do.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- weeds cannot grow after six weeks: Weeds can grow at any time; a well-grown crop simply shades them out.
- the crop needs no nutrients after six weeks: The crop needs nutrients until it matures.
- fertiliser can only be applied after weeding: Fertiliser can be applied at planting (basal) as well as later.

options.label: A
options.content: young crop plants are least able to compete with weeds for light, water and nutrients

options.label: B
options.content: weeds cannot grow after six weeks

options.label: C
options.content: the crop needs no nutrients after six weeks

options.label: D
options.content: fertiliser can only be applied after weeding

questions.stem: Seeds of crops such as groundnut are dressed with a fungicide or insecticide before planting in order to
questions.explanation:
Seed treatment is part of using good planting material: improved, certified seed of a suitable variety, free of pests and diseases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- break the dormancy of the seed: Dormancy is broken by scarification or soaking, not by seed dressing.
- supply nitrogen to the young plant: Seed dressings are pesticides, not fertilisers.
- make the seeds germinate faster: Seed dressing protects the seed; it does not speed up germination.

options.label: A
options.content: break the dormancy of the seed

options.label: B
options.content: protect the seeds and seedlings from soil-borne pests and diseases

options.label: C
options.content: supply nitrogen to the young plant

papers.title: Plant Propagation and Nursery Management: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on plant propagation and nursery management, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An advantage of vegetative propagation over propagation by seed is that
questions.explanation:
Vegetative propagation keeps the good qualities of a selected parent and often gives earlier maturity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it produces new varieties through variation: Variation comes from sexual reproduction with seeds; vegetative propagation gives copies.
- the planting material is light and easy to store: Cuttings, suckers and tubers are bulky and perishable; seeds are light and store well.
- diseases are never carried to the new plants: Vegetative material often carries diseases, such as cassava mosaic in cuttings.

options.label: A
options.content: it produces new varieties through variation

options.label: B
options.content: the planting material is light and easy to store

options.label: C
options.content: the new plants are true to type, identical to the parent

options.label: D
options.content: diseases are never carried to the new plants

questions.stem: Plantain is usually propagated by
questions.explanation:
Suckers grow from the base of the parent plant. Tissue-culture plantlets are also used to give disease-free planting material.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- stem cuttings: Stem cuttings are used for cassava and sweet potato.
- corms: Corms are used for cocoyam.
- seeds: Plantain does not produce viable seeds for planting.

questions.stem: In budding, as used for citrus,
questions.explanation:
T-budding is common in citrus. The bud and rootstock must be compatible, their cambium layers must touch, and the union must be tied firmly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a shoot with several buds is joined to a rootstock: Joining a shoot (scion) with several buds is grafting, used for mango.
- a branch is made to root while still attached to the parent: Rooting a branch while it is still attached is layering.
- a piece of stem is planted directly in the soil: Planting a piece of stem is propagation by stem cuttings.

options.label: A
options.content: a single bud from the desired variety is joined to a rootstock

options.label: B
options.content: a shoot with several buds is joined to a rootstock

options.label: C
options.content: a branch is made to root while still attached to the parent

options.label: D
options.content: a piece of stem is planted directly in the soil

questions.stem: For a graft to succeed, the cambium of the scion and the rootstock must be in contact because
questions.explanation:
When the two cambium layers touch, their new cells grow together and form a continuous link of xylem and phloem between stock and scion.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the cambium stores the food the scion needs: The cambium is a layer of dividing cells, not a food store.
- the cambium carries water from the roots: Water is carried by the xylem.
- the cambium contains the chlorophyll: The cambium does not photosynthesise.

options.label: A
options.content: the cambium stores the food the scion needs

options.label: B
options.content: the cambium is the tissue that divides to unite the two parts

options.label: C
options.content: the cambium carries water from the roots

questions.stem: A farmer tests 150 maize seeds on damp paper. After seven days, 120 have germinated. What is the germination percentage?
questions.explanation:
Germination % = (seeds germinated ÷ seeds tested) × 100 = (120 ÷ 150) × 100 = 80%. The farmer should sow more seed per hectare to allow for the 20% that fail.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20%: 20% is the percentage of seeds that failed to germinate.
- 120%: This writes the number of seeds that germinated as a percentage; it must be divided by the number tested.
- 125%: This divides 150 by 120, the wrong way round; a germination percentage cannot be more than 100%.

questions.stem: Seed dormancy caused by a hard seed coat can be broken by
questions.explanation:
Scarification or soaking lets water reach the embryo, so the seed can germinate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- drying the seeds in the sun: Drying does not soften a hard coat; it can make it harder.
- storing the seeds in a sealed container: Storage keeps seeds viable; it does not break dormancy caused by the coat.
- dressing the seeds with a fungicide: Seed dressing protects seeds from disease; it does not break dormancy.

options.label: A
options.content: drying the seeds in the sun

options.label: B
options.content: storing the seeds in a sealed container

options.label: C
options.content: scarification: nicking or rubbing the seed coat

options.label: D
options.content: dressing the seeds with a fungicide

questions.stem: Why are crops such as cocoa, oil palm and pepper first raised in a nursery?
questions.explanation:
In a nursery, seedlings are protected from strong sun, heavy rain, pests and weeds. Cocoa and oil palm are raised in polybags; tomato and pepper in beds or boxes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Nursery seedlings never need to be watered: Nursery seedlings need regular watering.
- A nursery makes the plants bear fruit without pollination: Raising seedlings in a nursery does not change how they produce fruit.
- Planting from a nursery needs more land than direct sowing: A nursery uses land efficiently: the field can be prepared, or used for something else, while seedlings grow.

options.label: A
options.content: Nursery seedlings never need to be watered

options.label: B
options.content: A nursery makes the plants bear fruit without pollination

options.label: C
options.content: Planting from a nursery needs more land than direct sowing

options.label: D
options.content: Young seedlings can be given special care and protection, and only the strongest are planted out

questions.stem: Swamp rice seedlings in Sierra Leone are usually transplanted from the nursery at about
questions.explanation:
Two or three seedlings are planted per hill. Transplanting at the right age gives a quick recovery and good tillering.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 days old: At 3 days the seedlings are far too small and weak to survive in the field.
- 3 months old: At 3 months the rice would be nearly mature; old seedlings recover poorly after transplanting.
- 1 year old: Rice is an annual crop; it completes its life cycle in a few months.

papers.title: Cereal Crops: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on cereal crops, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The scientific name of African rice is
questions.explanation:
Crossing African and Asian rice produced NERICA varieties, which combine hardiness with higher yield.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- *Oryza sativa*: *Oryza sativa* is Asian rice.
- *Zea mays*: *Zea mays* is maize.
- *Sorghum bicolor*: *Sorghum bicolor* is sorghum (guinea corn).

questions.stem: Which rice ecology in Sierra Leone can usually be cropped every year, and sometimes twice a year, without a fallow?
questions.explanation:
With bunds and channels, an inland valley swamp keeps the right depth of water and controls weeds by flooding, so rice can be grown every year.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Upland: Upland rice is grown on leached slopes that must rest after one or two crops.
- Boliland: Bolilands are seasonally flooded; yields are moderate and cropping depends on the floods.
- Riverine grassland: Riverine grasslands are flood plains whose cropping depends on the river's flood.

questions.stem: Rice plants have 'dead hearts' and produce white, empty heads. The pest most likely responsible is the
questions.explanation:
Stem borer larvae tunnel inside the stem, killing the central shoot (dead heart) or the panicle (white head). Destroying stubble after harvest removes larvae that would carry over.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- African rice gall midge: The gall midge makes onion-like tubes (galls) instead of panicles.
- rice bug: Rice bugs suck the developing grains, leaving them empty, but do not cause dead hearts.
- weaver bird: Weaver birds eat the ripening grain; they do not kill the central shoot.

questions.stem: Parboiling rice before milling
questions.explanation:
Parboiling is soaking the paddy, steaming it and drying it before milling. Much of the rice in Sierra Leone is parboiled.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- removes the husk from the grain: The husk is removed by milling, after parboiling.
- separates the grain from the straw: Separating grain from straw is threshing.
- removes the chaff by wind: Removing chaff by wind is winnowing.

options.label: A
options.content: removes the husk from the grain

options.label: B
options.content: separates the grain from the straw

options.label: D
options.content: hardens the grain so fewer grains break, keeps more nutrients and improves storage

questions.stem: Grain should be dried to a moisture content of about 12 to 14% before storage in order to
questions.explanation:
Damp grain heats up and goes mouldy, and insects multiply quickly in it. Well-dried grain in clean, dry, rat-proof stores keeps for months.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- make it germinate in the store: Damp grain may sprout in store; drying prevents this.
- increase its weight for sale: Drying reduces the weight, because water is removed.
- make it easier to thresh after storage: Threshing is done before storage, not after.

options.label: A
options.content: prevent moulds and storage insects from damaging it

options.label: B
options.content: make it germinate in the store

options.label: D
options.content: make it easier to thresh after storage

questions.stem: Maize streak disease, which causes yellow streaks on the leaves, is
questions.explanation:
Control: resistant varieties, timely planting and removing infected plants early.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a fungal disease spread by rain splash: Rain splash spreads fungal diseases such as cocoa black pod.
- caused by a shortage of nitrogen: Nitrogen shortage yellows older leaves evenly; it is not an infectious disease.
- caused by stem borers tunnelling in the stem: Stem borers cause dead hearts and broken stems, not streaks.

options.label: A
options.content: a fungal disease spread by rain splash

options.label: B
options.content: a virus disease spread by leafhoppers

options.label: C
options.content: caused by a shortage of nitrogen

options.label: D
options.content: caused by stem borers tunnelling in the stem

questions.stem: The fall armyworm is a serious pest of maize. Its damage is recognised by
questions.explanation:
The caterpillars feed inside the funnel of young leaves (the whorl). Scouting fields early and acting quickly limits the damage.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- onion-like tubes in place of the tassels: Onion-like tubes are made by the gall midge on rice.
- small round holes in stored grain: Holes in stored grain are made by weevils.
- yellow streaks along the leaves: Yellow streaks are a sign of maize streak virus.

options.label: A
options.content: onion-like tubes in place of the tassels

options.label: B
options.content: small round holes in stored grain

options.label: C
options.content: ragged holes in the leaves and droppings in the whorl

questions.stem: Maize is especially important as an animal feed because it is used in large amounts in feeds for
questions.explanation:
Ground maize supplies most of the energy in broiler and layer feeds, so the poultry industry depends heavily on maize.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cattle grazing on pasture: Grazing cattle feed mainly on grass; grain is a small part of their diet.
- goats browsing in the bush: Goats feed mainly by browsing shrubs and grasses.
- fish in the sea: Wild sea fish are not fed by farmers.

papers.title: Legumes, Roots, and Tubers: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on legumes, roots, and tubers, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Legumes such as groundnut and cowpea improve soil fertility because
questions.explanation:
This is why legumes are grown in rotation or intercropped with heavy feeders such as maize and cassava.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- their leaves contain a great deal of potassium: The benefit of legumes comes from nitrogen fixation, not potassium.
- their roots dissolve the rocks to release phosphorus: Legume roots do not dissolve rock.
- they are never attacked by pests: Legumes are attacked by many pests, such as aphids and pod borers.

options.label: A
options.content: *Rhizobium* bacteria in their root nodules fix nitrogen from the air

options.label: B
options.content: their leaves contain a great deal of potassium

options.label: C
options.content: their roots dissolve the rocks to release phosphorus

options.label: D
options.content: they are never attacked by pests

questions.stem: Cassava is propagated by
questions.explanation:
Cuttings should be taken only from healthy plants, because cassava mosaic virus is carried inside the stem.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- seeds: Cassava is not grown from seed by farmers.
- setts or minisetts: Setts and minisetts are pieces of tuber used to propagate yam.
- corms: Corms are used to propagate cocoyam.

questions.stem: Yam vines are trained up stakes mainly so that
questions.explanation:
More light means more photosynthesis, so more food is stored in the tuber.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the tubers grow above the ground: Yam tubers grow underground, whether or not the vines are staked.
- rats cannot reach the tubers: Staking the vines does not protect the tubers from rats.
- the vines do not need any fertiliser: Staking does not replace the need for nutrients.

options.label: A
options.content: the tubers grow above the ground

options.label: C
options.content: the leaves receive more light, which increases tuber yield

options.label: D
options.content: the vines do not need any fertiliser

questions.stem: Which of these crops is grown in Sierra Leone as much for its leaves, used in sauce, as for its roots?
questions.explanation:
Potato leaf sauce and cassava leaf sauce, cooked with palm oil, are everyday dishes, so both crops are valued for their leaves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Yam: Yam is grown for its tubers.
- Groundnut: Groundnut is grown for its seeds; the haulms are fed to animals.
- Ginger: Ginger is grown for its rhizomes.

questions.stem: In making gari, grated cassava is pressed after fermentation and then
questions.explanation:
Gari: peel, wash, grate, ferment for 2 to 3 days, press out the liquid, sieve, roast. Processing removes most of the poisonous cyanide compounds.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- soaked in water for several days: Soaking for several days is how fufu is made.
- sliced and sun-dried into chips: Sun-dried slices make cassava chips and flour.
- washed to separate out the starch: Washing out and settling the starch makes cassava starch.

options.label: B
options.content: soaked in water for several days

options.label: D
options.content: washed to separate out the starch

questions.stem: Which crop is a legume?
questions.explanation:
Legumes have pods and root nodules. Groundnut, cowpea, soya bean, pigeon pea and bambara groundnut are grain legumes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cassava: Cassava is a root crop.
- Cocoyam: Cocoyam is grown for its corms; it is not a legume.
- Sorghum: Sorghum is a cereal.

questions.stem: Small pieces of yam tuber of about 25 to 50 g, dusted with ash or fungicide before planting, are called
questions.explanation:
Minisetts save tubers that would otherwise be used as planting material, leaving more to eat or sell. The ash or fungicide protects the cut surfaces from rot.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- suckers: Suckers are shoots from the base of plants such as plantain.
- slips: Slips are shoots used to propagate pineapple.
- vine cuttings: Vine cuttings are used for sweet potato.

papers.title: Plantation and Cash Crops: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on plantation and cash crops, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In Sierra Leone, cocoa and coffee are grown mainly in the
questions.explanation:
The forested east has the deep soils, rainfall and humidity cocoa and coffee need; cashew is spreading in the north.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Western Area peninsula: The Western Area is too small and built up for large cocoa and coffee production.
- bolilands of the north: The bolilands are seasonally flooded grasslands used mainly for rice.
- mangrove swamps of the coast: Cocoa and coffee cannot grow in salty tidal swamps.

options.label: D
options.content: east, in Kailahun, Kenema and Kono

questions.stem: Cocoa beans are fermented after harvest mainly to
questions.explanation:
Fermentation kills the germ, removes the sticky pulp and starts the chemical changes that produce chocolate flavour. Poorly fermented beans are graded down.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- make the beans germinate before sale: Fermentation kills the embryo, so the beans cannot germinate.
- increase the weight of the beans: Fermentation and drying reduce the weight of the beans.
- kill the mirids on the pods: Mirids are controlled in the field; fermentation is done on harvested beans.

options.label: A
options.content: develop the chocolate flavour and brown colour of the beans

options.label: B
options.content: make the beans germinate before sale

options.label: C
options.content: increase the weight of the beans

options.label: D
options.content: kill the mirids on the pods

questions.stem: Black pod disease of cocoa, in which the pods rot brown-black in wet weather, is caused by
questions.explanation:
Control: harvest often, remove and destroy infected pods, prune to let air move through the trees, and spray copper fungicides.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a virus spread by mealybugs: A virus spread by mealybugs causes cocoa swollen shoot disease.
- sap-sucking mirids: Mirids cause black patches and dieback of branches.
- a shortage of potassium: Potassium shortage scorches leaf edges; it is not an infectious disease.

questions.stem: The oil palm type planted on modern farms, which has a thin shell and the most oil, is
questions.explanation:
Tenera is the hybrid Dura × Pisifera. Its thick mesocarp holds more oil, so it gives the highest yields.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Dura: Dura has a thick shell and less oil; it is common in wild groves.
- Pisifera: Pisifera has no shell, but its female flowers are usually sterile; it is used as the male parent.
- Cocos: *Cocos nucifera* is the coconut palm, not a type of oil palm.

questions.stem: Cashew trees are grown for
questions.explanation:
Cashew is increasingly planted, especially in the north, and is a growing source of export income.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- latex for making rubber: Latex comes from the rubber tree.
- rhizomes that are dried and exported: Dried rhizomes come from ginger.
- beans that are fermented to make chocolate: Fermented beans for chocolate come from cocoa.

options.label: B
options.content: rhizomes that are dried and exported

options.label: C
options.content: beans that are fermented to make chocolate

options.label: D
options.content: their nuts for export, and their 'apples' for juice

questions.stem: Which of the following is a problem of cash-crop production in Sierra Leone?
questions.explanation:
Other problems include old, low-yielding trees, pests and diseases, the long wait for the first harvest and competition with food crops for land and labour.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cash crops bring in no foreign exchange: Cash crops earn foreign exchange; that is one of their main benefits.
- Cash crops are ready to harvest in a few weeks: Tree crops take years to bear; the long wait is a problem, not a quick harvest.
- Cash crops create no employment: Cash crops employ many people in farming, processing and trade.

options.label: A
options.content: Prices on world markets rise and fall, so farmers' incomes are uncertain

options.label: B
options.content: Cash crops bring in no foreign exchange

options.label: C
options.content: Cash crops are ready to harvest in a few weeks

questions.stem: Cocoa beans should be dried on raised platforms or mats rather than on the roadside because beans dried on the road
questions.explanation:
Clean, well-fermented, well-dried beans fetch the best price.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dry too slowly in the sun: Drying speed is not the problem; contamination is.
- lose their chocolate flavour by fermenting again: Beans do not ferment again once they are drying.
- become too heavy to sell: Dirt is not the main problem because of weight; it lowers quality and price.

options.label: A
options.content: dry too slowly in the sun

options.label: B
options.content: pick up dirt and smells and may go mouldy, so they are graded down

options.label: C
options.content: lose their chocolate flavour by fermenting again

questions.stem: Cocoa trees infected with swollen shoot virus must be cut out because
questions.explanation:
Removing infected trees, and replanting with healthy material, stops the virus spreading through the farm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the trees will recover if they are cut back: Infected trees do not recover; cutting back does not remove the virus.
- swollen shoot is caused by too much shade: Swollen shoot is a virus disease, not a result of shade.
- fungicides make the disease worse: Fungicides act on fungi; they have no effect on a virus.

options.label: A
options.content: the trees will recover if they are cut back

options.label: B
options.content: swollen shoot is caused by too much shade

options.label: C
options.content: the virus cannot be cured, and infected trees spread it through mealybugs to healthy trees

papers.title: Vegetable and Fruit Production: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on vegetable and fruit production, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of these is a fruit vegetable?
questions.explanation:
Fruit vegetables are eaten as fruits: pepper, tomato, okra, garden egg, cucumber and pumpkin.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Krain-krain: Krain-krain (jute mallow) is a leafy vegetable.
- Onion: Onion is a bulb vegetable.
- Carrot: Carrot is a root vegetable.

questions.stem: Vegetables are often grown on raised beds about 1 m wide because raised beds
questions.explanation:
A bed about 1 m wide can be reached from both sides without stepping on the soil, so its structure is kept loose.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- need no organic manure: Vegetables on raised beds still need plenty of organic matter.
- stop all pests reaching the plants: Raised beds do not keep pests away.
- allow tractors to work between the plants: Beds are made for hand work; their width lets the gardener reach the middle from each side.

options.label: A
options.content: drain well in the rains and are easy to water and weed

options.label: C
options.content: stop all pests reaching the plants

options.label: D
options.content: allow tractors to work between the plants

questions.stem: Which vegetable is usually raised in a nursery and then transplanted?
questions.explanation:
Tomato, pepper, garden egg, cabbage, lettuce and onion are raised in a nursery and transplanted at about 4 to 6 weeks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Okra: Okra is usually sown directly in the bed.
- Cucumber: Cucumber is usually sown directly.
- Krain-krain: Krain-krain is usually sown directly.

questions.stem: Tomato, pepper and garden egg should not follow one another in the same bed, season after season, because they
questions.explanation:
Rotating with crops of a different family, such as leafy vegetables or legumes, starves out the pests and pathogens.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- need completely different soils: They grow in similar soils; the problem is shared pests and diseases.
- can only be grown in the dry season: These vegetables can be grown in the rains as well as in the dry season.
- poison the soil for one another: They do not poison the soil; disease organisms build up in it.

options.label: B
options.content: can only be grown in the dry season

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Mango is usually propagated by grafting rather than by seed because
questions.explanation:
Grafted mango trees bear in 3 to 5 years and are true to type. Citrus is propagated by budding for the same reasons.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mango seeds never germinate: Mango seeds germinate well; the problem is that seedlings take long to bear and vary.
- grafted trees need no care after planting: Grafted trees still need watering, weeding and the removal of rootstock shoots.
- seedling trees cannot produce fruit at all: Seedling trees do bear, but only after many years, and their fruit varies.

options.label: B
options.content: grafted trees need no care after planting

options.label: C
options.content: seedling trees cannot produce fruit at all

options.label: D
options.content: grafted trees bear earlier and give fruit of the same quality as the parent

questions.stem: Pineapple is propagated by
questions.explanation:
The first fruit is ready at about 15 to 20 months, and flowering can be induced so that the harvest is uniform.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- budding onto a rootstock: Budding is used for citrus.
- stem cuttings: Stem cuttings are used for cassava.
- seeds: Pineapple is not grown from seed by farmers.

questions.stem: Which practice best reduces post-harvest losses of tomatoes taken to market?
questions.explanation:
Gentle handling, crates instead of sacks, shade and quick transport keep vegetables fresh; drying and processing reduce losses further.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Packing them tightly in sacks: Sacks crush the fruit, and bruised tomatoes rot quickly.
- Leaving them in the sun to ripen evenly: Sun heats the fruit and speeds up rotting.
- Harvesting them in the hottest part of the day: Fruit picked in the heat spoils faster.

options.label: B
options.content: Picking in the cool morning, packing in crates and transporting quickly

options.label: C
options.content: Leaving them in the sun to ripen evenly

options.label: D
options.content: Harvesting them in the hottest part of the day
